holidays.name: National Candy Cane Day
holidays.description: Time to unwrap that striped peppermint hook. People mark the day by eating candy canes, hanging them on trees, stirring them into hot cocoa, or crushing them over ice cream. It's a good way to use up the leftover Christmas candy.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It falls the day after Christmas, when candy canes are everywhere.
holidays.funFact: Candy canes are often said to have started as bent sticks of sugar candy. Folklore says a choirmaster handed them out to keep children quiet during long services.

holidays.name: National Whiners' Day
holidays.description: This is the day to groan about every disappointment from the holidays. Think scratchy sweaters, the wrong size, a third fruitcake, and a gift receipt you can't find. It gives you a day to complain out loud before the new year starts.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It is meant as a playful release for post-holiday letdowns.
holidays.funFact: It sits right next to Boxing Day and National Returns Day, so you can complain and then take the offending gift back to the store.

holidays.name: National Thank-You Note Day
holidays.description: This day asks you to swap a quick text for pen and paper. You write real thank-you notes for the gifts you got. A handwritten note can make someone's week, and it clears your gratitude to-do list before New Year's.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It lands right after the gift-giving rush, when thank-you notes are most needed.
holidays.funFact: Handwritten thank-you notes are now rare enough that the people who get them tend to remember them.
